extracted.intended_audience: general readers; educators and researchers interested in media literacy, misinformation, and game-based interventions
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style descriptive entry about a single browser-based 'newsgame' (Bad News) that aims to improve media literacy by letting players adopt the role of a fake-news producer; includes gameplay, theoretical basis, evaluation, awards, and localization. Useful for readers learning what the game is and how it was designed and evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: immunize public against misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of the game is to immunize the public against misinformation by letting players take on the role of a fake news producer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing the game's objective explicitly around 'immunizing' the public situates it as an intervention for media literacy and social impact rather than pure entertainment. Use of the term signals that success should be measured by changes in players' susceptibility to misinformation or improved discernment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role-play mechanic: perspective of a fake news tycoon
rubrics_metrics.description: Players take the perspective of a fake news tycoon (i.e., 'take on the role of a fake news producer').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choice: role-play as the misinformation producer to expose players to how deceptive techniques are used. This mechanic is intended to teach by doing — 'Spot Fake News By Making It' — and suggests assessment via engagement and learning outcomes rather than only scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Badge system representing common fake-news techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Players earn 'badges', each of which correspond to common techniques used in the production of fake news, such as polarization, conspiracy theories, discrediting, trolling, and invoking emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The badge taxonomy enumerates specific tactics that the game deliberately exposes players to. As a production/evaluation criterion, include clear mappings from badges to concrete techniques and ensure the game demonstrates these techniques in weakened/educational form. Tests of effectiveness can measure recognition of these named tactics after play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gameplay goal: build a fake-news empire while maintaining credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal is to build your own fake news empire and gain as many followers as possible while maintaining credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates a pedagogical tension (persuasion vs. credibility) central to the game's learning objectives. Evaluation metrics can include players' ability to manipulate credibility trade-offs, and whether experiencing that trade-off improves later detection of similar strategies in real media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical basis: inoculation theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The game is based on a psychological concept known as inoculation theory, where exposure to weakened doses of common fake news tactics is thought to help confer resistance or psychological immunity against fake news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and evaluation should be aligned with inoculation theory: present attenuated examples of persuasive techniques, then test whether that exposure reduces susceptibility. Scientific evaluation should reference inoculation-theory outcomes (e.g., reduced belief in misinformation, improved discernment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based evaluation: subject of scientific research
rubrics_metrics.description: The game has been the subject of scientific research evaluating its impact on fake news discernment and recognition (several peer-reviewed studies cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an evaluative standard, effectiveness should be demonstrated via empirical studies (pre/post measures, control groups, validated instruments). The page cites multiple journal articles (Journal of Risk Research; Palgrave Communications; Journal of Cognition; Harvard Kennedy School Misinformation Review; Educational and Psychological Measurement), which can serve as models for appropriate research designs and outcome measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and impact: awards and exhibits as validation signals
rubrics_metrics.description: The game received awards (2020 Brouwers Trust Prize; Frank Prize in Public Interest Communications) and was exhibited (Design Museum, Museum of Discovery), indicating external recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awards, exhibitions, and institutional recognition are listed as additional indicators of social impact and design quality. While not substitutes for controlled evaluation, such honors can be used as supplementary evidence of reach and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization/adaptation for specific disinformation contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2020, localised versions of the game were released for Eastern European markets where Russian-backed disinformation is of particular concern; Debunk.org published multiple-language versions in Russian, Lithuanian, Latvian, Estonian and Polish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a production criterion, adapt content linguistically and culturally to the regional vectors of misinformation. Localization should target region-specific narratives and threat actors to maximize relevance and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and distribution: free browser platform
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad News is a free browser game (platform: Browser; released February 19, 2018).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribution as a free browser-based experience is a design decision aimed at broad accessibility and uptake. Evaluation of reach and public impact should consider platform accessibility (no install barrier) and potential limitations (requires browser, internet access).
